ref-2e5ce0b63b29a50bf2af.text: Raspberry Robin uses rundll32 execution without any command line parameters to contact command and control infrastructure, such as IP addresses associated with Tor nodes. Raspberry Robin retrieves its second stage payload in a variety of ways such as through msiexec.exe abuse, or running the curl command to download the payload to the victim's %AppData% folder. Raspberry Robin uses newly-registered domains containing only a few characters for command and controll purposes, such as "v0[.]cx". Raspberry Robin uses regsvr32.exe execution without any command line parameters for command and control requests to IP addresses associated with Tor nodes. Raspberry Robin uses mixed-case letters for filenames and commands to evade detection. Raspberry Robin uses msiexec.exe for post-installation communication to command and control infrastructure. Msiexec.exe is executed referencing a remote resource for second-stage payload retrieval and execution. Raspberry Robin uses the Windows utility odbcconf.exe to execute malicious commands, using the regsvr flag to execute DLLs and bypass application control mechanisms that are not monitoring for odbcconf.exe abuse. Raspberry Robin is capable of contacting the TOR network for delivering second-stage payloads. Raspberry Robin has historically been delivered via infected USB drives containing a malicious LNK object masquerading as a legitimate folder. Raspberry Robin uses cmd.exe to read and execute a file stored on an infected USB device as part of initial installation. Raspberry Robin will communicate via HTTP over port 8080 for command and control traffic. Raspberry Robin uses outbound HTTP requests containing victim information for retrieving second stage payloads. Variants of Raspberry Robin can download archive files (such as 7-Zip files) via the victim web browser for second stage execution. Raspberry Robin has historically used infected USB media to spread to new victims. Raspberry Robin will use the legitimate Windows utility fodhelper.exe to run processes at elevated privileges without requiring a User Account Control prompt.

TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can search GitHub for Actions runner processes.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can compress and encrypt data and exfiltrate it via POST to an attacker-controlled domain. If that method fails it can use the victim's own GitHub account to create a public repository and uploads the encrypted data as a release asset.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has searched victim hosts for TLS and SSH keys.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has searched for cryptocurrency wallets on targeted hosts.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can harvest credentials from cryptocurrency wallets and keystores such as Ethereum keystores, Cardano keys, Solana validator keypairs, Ledger device files, and Anchor deploy keys.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can create a repository in the victim's GitHub account using the victim's own GITHUB_TOKEN to upload stolen credentials.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can locate GitHub Actions runner processes.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can scrape memory from the Runner.Worker process by reading `/proc/<pid>/mem` to extract secrets including plaintext tokens.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has used multi-stage payloads with double Base64-encoded scripts to evade static analysis.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has encrypted collected data using a hybrid RSA-4096 and AES-256-encryption prior to exfiltration over 'curl`.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has encrypted collected data using a hybrid AES-256 and RSA-4096 encryption prior to exfiltration over 'curl`.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can search filesystems for cryptocurrency wallets such as Bitcoin, Litecoin, Dogecoin, Zcash, Dash, Ripple, and Monero.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can identify files containing environment variables, SSH keys, cloud credentials, access tokens, and cryptocurrency wallets.

ref-9a160e23c7da35c0f4d7.text: Stuxnet attempts to impersonate an anonymous token to enumerate bindings in the service control manager. Stuxnet uses encrypted configuration blocks and writes encrypted files to disk. Stuxnet transforms encrypted binary data into an ASCII string in order to use it as a URL parameter value. Stuxnet encodes the payload of system information sent to the command and control servers using a one byte 0xFF XOR key. Stuxnet also uses a 31-byte long static byte string to XOR data sent to command and control servers. The servers use a different static key to encrypt replies to the implant. Stuxnet enumerates user accounts of the local host. Stuxnet collects the IP address of a compromised system. Stuxnet uses a driver registered as a boot start service as the main load-point. Stuxnet calls LoadLibrary then executes exports from a DLL. Stuxnet infects remote servers via network shares and by infecting WinCC database views with malicious code. Stuxnet uses the SetSecurityDescriptorDacl API to reduce object integrity levels. Stuxnet enumerates the directories of a network resource. Stuxnet used MS10-073 and an undisclosed Task Scheduler vulnerability to escalate privileges on local Windows machines. Stuxnet can propagate via peer-to-peer communication and updates using RPC. Stuxnet used xp_cmdshell to store and execute SQL code. Stuxnet reduces the integrity level of objects to allow write actions. Stuxnet extracts and writes driver files that match the times of other legitimate files. Stuxnet decrypts resources that are loaded into memory and executed. Stuxnet can create registry keys to load driver files. Stuxnet propagates using the MS10-061 Print Spooler and MS08-067 Windows Server Service vulnerabilities. Stuxnet used WMI with an explorer.exe token to execute on a remote share. Stuxnet attempts to access network resources with a domain account’s credentials. Stuxnet can propagate via removable media using an autorun.inf file or the CVE-2010-2568 LNK vulnerability. Stuxnet infected WinCC machines via a hardcoded database server password. Stuxnet enumerates removable drives for infection. Stuxnet used a digitally signed driver with a compromised Realtek certificate. Stuxnet checks for specific operating systems on 32-bit machines, Registry keys, and dates for vulnerabilities, and will exit execution if the values are not met. Stuxnet collects system information including computer and domain names, OS version, and S7P paths. Stuxnet enumerates the currently running processes related to a variety of security products. Stuxnet uses a driver to scan for specific filesystem driver objects. Stuxnet schedules a network job to execute two minutes after host infection. Stuxnet uses HTTP to communicate with a command and control server. Stuxnet installs an RPC server for P2P communications. Stuxnet propagates to available network shares. Stuxnet enumerates user accounts of the domain. Stuxnet encrypts exfiltrated data via C2 with static 31-byte long XOR keys. Stuxnet sends compromised victim information via HTTP. Stuxnet injects an entire DLL into an existing, newly created, or preselected trusted process. Stuxnet uses an RPC server that contains a file dropping routine and support for payload version updates for P2P communications within a victim network. Stuxnet collects the time and date of a system when it is infected. Stuxnet uses an RPC server that contains a routine for file deletion and also removes itself from the system through a DLL export by deleting specific files. Stuxnet searches the Registry for indicators of security programs. Stuxnet uses a Windows rootkit to mask its binaries and other relevant files. Stuxnet has the ability to generate new C2 domains. Stuxnet can delete OLE Automation and SQL stored procedures used to store malicious payloads.
ref-9a160e23c7da35c0f4d7.title: Nicolas Falliere, Liam O Murchu, Eric Chien 2011, February W32.Stuxnet Dossier (Version 1.4) Retrieved November 17, 2024.

ref-a21951667463c7d8b15e.text:
ODAgent can use the Microsoft Graph API to access an attacker-controlled OneDrive account and retrieve payloads and backdoor commands.
OilCheck can download staged payloads from an actor-controlled infrastructure.
OilBooster can download and execute files from an actor-controlled OneDrive account.
OilBooster can hide its console window upon execution through the `ShowWindow` API.
OilBooster has the ability to execute shell commands and exfiltrate the results.
OilBooster can use the OpenSSL library to encrypt C2 communications.
SampleCheck5000 can use the Microsoft Office Exchange Web Services API to access an actor-controlled account and retrieve C2 commands and payloads placed in Draft messages.
SampleCheck5000 can gzip compress files uploaded to a shared mailbox used for C2 and exfiltration.
ODAgent can Base64-decode and XOR decrypt received C2 commands.
OilBooster can identify the compromised system's hostname which is used to create a unique identifier.
OilBooster can stage files in the `tempFiles` directory for exfiltration.
SampleCheck5000 can create unique victim identifiers by using the compromised system’s volume ID.
ODAgent can use an attacker-controlled OneDrive account to receive C2 commands and to exfiltrate files.
ODAgent can delete payloads and files used to pass C2 commands from remotely hosted cloud accounts.
ODAgent can identify the current working directory.
OilCheck can upload documents from compromised hosts to a shared Microsoft Office 365 Outlook email account for exfiltration.
OilBooster can send HTTP `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` requests to the Microsoft Graph API over port 443 for C2 communication.
OilBooster can Base64-decode and XOR-decrypt C2 commands taken from JSON files.
OilBooster has used the `ShowWindow` and `CreateProcessW` APIs.
ODAgent can execute a specified command line passed via API.
OilBooster can exfiltrate files to an actor-controlled OneDrive account via the Microsoft Graph API.
OilBooster can use an actor-controlled OneDrive account for C2 communication and exfiltration.
SampleCheck5000 can download additional payloads to compromised hosts.
SampleCheck5000 can use the Exchange Web Services API for C2 communication.
SampleCheck5000 can use the Microsoft Office Exchange Web Services API to access an actor-controlled account and retrieve files for exfiltration.
ODAgent can pass commands using native APIs.
OilBooster can identify the compromised system's username which is then used as part of a unique identifier.
OilBooster can use a backup channel to request a new refresh token from its C2 server after 10 consecutive unsuccessful connections to the primary OneDrive C2 server.
SampleCheck5000 can log the output from C2 commands in an encrypted and compressed format on disk prior to exfiltration.
OilBooster can read the results of command line execution via an unnamed pipe connected to the process.
SampleCheck5000 can create unique victim identifiers by using the compromised system’s computer name.
ODAgent has the ability to download and execute files on compromised systems.
ODAgent can use an attacker-controlled OneDrive account for exfiltration.
OilBooster uses the Microsoft Graph API to connect to an actor-controlled OneDrive account to download and execute files and shell commands, and to create directories to share exfiltrated data.
SampleCheck5000 can decode and decrypt command line strings and files received through C2.
OilCheck can use a REST-based Microsoft Graph API to access draft messages in a shared Microsoft Office 365 Outlook email account used for C2 communication.
SampleCheck5000 can call cmd.exe to execute C2 command line strings.
ref-a21951667463c7d8b15e.title: Hromcova, Z. and Burgher, A. (2023, December 14). OilRig’s persistent attacks using cloud service-powered downloaders. Retrieved November 26, 2024.

ref-b69fafa9bf9e59c2eeb9.text:
Sys10 collects the computer name, OS versioning information, and OS install date and sends the information to the C2.
WinMM sets a WH_CBT Windows hook to search for and capture files on the victim.
Sys10 collects the group name of the logged-in user and sends it to the C2.
WinMM is usually configured with primary and backup domains for C2 communications.
HDoor scans to identify open ports on the victim.
WinMM uses NetUser-GetInfo to identify that it is running under an “Admin” account on the local system.
SslMM has a hard-coded primary and backup C2 string.
Sys10 collects the local IP address of the victim and sends it to the C2.
HDoor kills anti-virus found on the victim.
WinMM sets a WH_CBT Windows hook to collect information on process creation.
WinMM uses HTTP for C2.
To establish persistence, SslMM identifies the Start Menu Startup directory and drops a link to its own executable disguised as an “Office Start,” “Yahoo Talk,” “MSN Gaming Z0ne,” or “MSN Talk” shortcut.
SslMM identifies and kills anti-malware processes.
WinMM collects the system name, OS version including service pack, and system install date and sends the information to the C2 server.
Sys10 collects the account name of the logged-in user and sends it to the C2.
Sys10 uses an XOR 0x1 loop to encrypt its C2 domain.
SslMM sends the logged-on username to its hard-coded C2.
Sys10 uses HTTP for C2.
SslMM contains a feature to manipulate process privileges and tokens.
SslMM creates a new thread implementing a keylogging facility using Windows Keyboard Accelerators.
SslMM sends information to its hard-coded C2, including OS version, service pack information, processor speed, system name, and OS install date.

ref-b6e2fdea29b14182835a.text: GravityRAT has been delivered via Word documents using DDE for execution. GravityRAT collects the volumes mapped on the system, and also steals files with the following extensions: .docx, .doc, .pptx, .ppt, .xlsx, .xls, .rtf, and .pdf. GravityRAT collects the victim username along with other account information (account type, description, full name, SID and status). GravityRAT has used HTTP over a non-standard port, such as TCP port 46769. GravityRAT steals files with the following extensions: .docx, .doc, .pptx, .ppt, .xlsx, .xls, .rtf, and .pdf. GravityRAT steals files based on an extension list if a USB drive is connected to the system. GravityRAT uses WMI to check the BIOS and manufacturer information for strings like "VMWare", "Virtual", and "XEN" and another WMI request to get the current temperature of the hardware to determine if it's a virtual machine environment. GravityRAT supports file encryption (AES with the key "lolomycin2017"). GravityRAT can obtain the date and time of a system. GravityRAT uses the netstat command to find open ports on the victim’s machine. GravityRAT collects the MAC address, computer name, and CPU information. GravityRAT executes commands remotely on the infected host. GravityRAT creates a scheduled task to ensure it is re-executed everyday. GravityRAT lists the running processes on the system. GravityRAT collects the victim IP address, MAC address, as well as the victim account domain name. GravityRAT uses HTTP for C2. GravityRAT has a feature to list the available services on the system. The author of GravityRAT submitted samples to VirusTotal for testing, showing that the author modified the code to try to hide the DDE object in a different part of the document. GravityRAT collects various information via WMI requests, including CPU information in the Win32_Processor entry (Processor ID, Name, Manufacturer and the clock speed).
ref-b6e2fdea29b14182835a.title: Mercer, W., Rascagneres, P. (2018, April 26). GravityRAT - The Two-Year Evolution Of An APT Targeting India. Retrieved May 16, 2018.

BlackCat has the ability modify access tokens.
BlackCat has the ability to stop VM services on compromised networks.
BlackCat can change the desktop wallpaper on compromised hosts.
BlackCat has the ability to wipe VM snapshots on compromised networks.
BlackCat has the ability to discover network shares on compromised networks.

ref-da3f4df77e58001429a7.text:
Bankshot creates processes using the Windows API calls: CreateProcessA() and CreateProcessAsUserA().
Bankshot collects files from the local system.
Bankshot can terminate a specific process by its process id.
Bankshot marks files to be deleted upon the next system reboot and uninstalls and removes itself from the system.
Bankshot identifies processes and collects the process ids.
Bankshot recursively generates a list of files within a directory and sends them back to the control server.
Bankshot exfiltrates data over its C2 channel.
Bankshot encodes commands from the control server using a range of characters and gzip.
Bankshot uses HTTP for command and control communication.
Bankshot leverages a known zero-day vulnerability in Adobe Flash to execute the implant into the victims’ machines.
Bankshot gathers domain and account names/information through process monitoring.
Bankshot uses the command-line interface to execute arbitrary commands.
Bankshot modifies the time of a file as specified by the control server.
Bankshot gathers system information, network addresses, and the operation system version.
Bankshot grabs a user token using WTSQueryUserToken and then creates a process by impersonating a logged-on user.
Bankshot gathers disk type and disk free space.
ref-da3f4df77e58001429a7.title: Sherstobitoff, R. (2018, March 08). Hidden Cobra Targets Turkish Financial Sector With New Bankshot Implant. Retrieved May 18, 2018.

ref-f7e406422154c4f5f6f3.text: Cobalt Strike includes a capability to modify the Beacon payload to eliminate known signatures or unpacking methods. Cobalt Strike can enumerate services on compromised hosts. Cobalt Strike can explore files on a compromised system. Cobalt Strike can exploit vulnerabilities such as MS14-058. Cobalt Strike's Beacon payload is capable of capturing screenshots. Cobalt Strike can use Base64, URL-safe Base64, or NetBIOS encoding in its C2 traffic. Cobalt Strike can spawn a job to inject into LSASS memory and dump password hashes. Cobalt Strike uses a custom command and control protocol that is encapsulated in HTTP, HTTPS, or DNS. In addition, it conducts peer-to-peer communication over Windows named pipes encapsulated in the SMB protocol. All protocols use their standard assigned ports. Cobalt Strike can collect data from a local system. Cobalt Strike can use WinRM to execute a payload on a remote host. Cobalt Strike can track key presses with a keylogger module. Cobalt Strike can timestomp any files or payloads placed on a target machine to help them blend in. The Cobalt Strike System Profiler can discover applications through the browser and identify the version of Java the target has. Cobalt Strike can determine the NetBios name and the IP addresses of targets machines including domain controllers. Cobalt Strike's execute-assembly command can run a .NET executable within the memory of a sacrificial process by loading the CLR. Cobalt Strike can use process hollowing for execution. Cobalt Strike can use a number of known techniques to bypass Windows UAC. Cobalt Strike can identify targets by querying account groups on a domain contoller. Cobalt Strike can use spoof arguments in spawned processes that execute beacon commands. Cobalt Strike can use PsExec to execute a payload on a remote host. It can also use Service Control Manager to start new services. Cobalt Strike can be configured to have commands relayed over a peer-to-peer network of infected hosts. This can be used to limit the number of egress points, or provide access to a host without direct internet access. Cobalt Strike can perform browser pivoting and inject into a user's browser to inherit cookies, authenticated HTTP sessions, and client SSL certificates. Cobalt Strike has the ability to accept a value for HTTP Host Header to enable domain fronting. Cobalt Strike can steal access tokens from exiting processes. Cobalt Strike can SSH to a remote service. Cobalt Strike can use net localgroup to list local groups on a system. Cobalt Strike can use sudo to run a command.
ref-f7e406422154c4f5f6f3.title: Strategic Cyber LLC. (2020, November 5). Cobalt Strike: Advanced Threat Tactics for Penetration Testers. Retrieved April 13, 2021.

ref-fb2a494a1294f8ada722.text:
BlackCat can clear Windows event logs using `wevtutil.exe`.
BlackCat can use `wmic.exe` to delete shadow copies on compromised networks.
BlackCat can enumerate files for encryption.
BlackCat can utilize `net use` commands to identify domain users.
BlackCat can use Windows commands such as `fsutil behavior set SymLinkEvaluation R2L:1` to redirect file system access to a different location after gaining access into compromised networks.
BlackCat has the ability to add the following registry key on compromised networks to maintain persistence: `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services \LanmanServer\Paramenters`
BlackCat can utilize `net use` commands to discover the user name on a compromised host.
BlackCat can broadcasts NetBIOS Name Service (NBNC) messages to search for servers connected to compromised networks.
BlackCat can enumerate local drives.
BlackCat can obtain the computer name and UUID.
BlackCat can replicate itself across connected servers via `psexec`.
BlackCat can delete shadow copies using `vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet` and `wmic.exe Shadowcopy Delete`; it can also modify the boot loader using `bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled No`.
BlackCat can determine if a user on a compromised host has domain admin privileges.
BlackCat can execute commands on a compromised network with the use of `cmd.exe`.
BlackCat has the ability to encrypt Windows devices, Linux devices, and VMWare instances.
BlackCat can bypass UAC to escalate privileges.
ref-fb2a494a1294f8ada722.title: Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence. (2022, June 13). The many lives of BlackCat ransomware. Retrieved December 20, 2022.
